```{r table function, include=FALSE, echo = FALSE}

# A function to make the tables prettier for the jmv output. 
jtable<-function(jobject,digits=3) {
snames<-sapply(jobject$columns,function(a) a$title)
asDF<-jobject$asDF
tnames<-unlist(lapply(names(asDF) ,function(n) snames[[n]]))
names(asDF)<-tnames
kableExtra::kable(asDF,"html",
table.attr='class="jmv-results-table-table"',
row.names = F,
digits=3)
}
```



```{r import data, include = FALSE}
mainData <-  read_excel("Data_public.xls")

RTs_boxcox <- read_csv("RTs_after_boxcox.csv")

```
# Overall summary

For this paper, it was not possible to replicate any of the ERP analyses as ERP and EEG data were not provided. The only available data were Excel files with the summary ERP data and behavioural and reaction time data. These allowed all of the statistical analyses from the paper to be replicated. Interestingly, the Bayesian analyses reported in the "ERP Results" section are all one-sided, although this is not acknowledged in the text and all other reported analyses in the paper are two-sided. 

I used jamovi version 1.2.5.0 for the analyses, and pasted the syntax into RMarkdown using the jmv package. 

## Behavioural tasks


### Dot-probe tasks 
From the paper:

> A Wilcoxon signed rank test indicated no significant differences between RTs for congruent and incongruent trials in the masked dot-probe task, $W = 129.0, p = .06, BF = 2.13$ (alternative hypothesis 2.1 times more likely, anecdotal evidence for the alternative hypothesis).

These results can be seen as replicated in the table below. They are from the dataset called "RTs after boxcox" - the RTs in the main dataset do not produce these results, although they are similar. 

#### Masked trials 

```{r dot-probe masked trials, echo=FALSE, results = 'asis'}

masked_RTs_ttest_w <- jmv::ttestPS(
    data = RTs_boxcox,
    pairs = list(
        list(
            i1="RT_Uncon_Valid",
            i2="RT_Uncon_Inavlid")),
    students = FALSE,
    bf = FALSE,
    wilcoxon = TRUE)

masked_RTs_ttest_b <- jmv::ttestPS(
    data = RTs_boxcox,
    pairs = list(
        list(
            i1="RT_Uncon_Valid",
            i2="RT_Uncon_Inavlid")),
    students = FALSE,
    bf = TRUE)

cat("<pre class='jamovitable'>")
print(jtable(masked_RTs_ttest_w$ttest))
cat("</pre>")

cat("<pre class='jamovitable'>")
print(jtable(masked_RTs_ttest_b$ttest))
cat("</pre>")

```

From the paper: 

> RTs obtained in the unmasked dot-probe task did not differ between the congruent and incongruent trials, t(17) = −0.71, p = .487, BF = 0.30 (null hypothesis 3.3 times more likely, moderate evidence).

These are also replicated in the table below. 

#### Unmasked trials 

```{r dot-probe umasked trials, echo=FALSE, results = 'asis'}

unmasked_RTs_ttest_w <- jmv::ttestPS(
    data = RTs_boxcox,
    pairs = list(
        list(
            i1="RT_Con_Valid",
            i2="RT_Con_Invalid")),
    students = TRUE,
    wilcoxon = FALSE)

unmasked_RTs_ttest_b <- jmv::ttestPS(
    data = RTs_boxcox,
    pairs = list(
        list(
            i1="RT_Con_Valid",
            i2="RT_Con_Invalid")),
    students = FALSE,
    bf = TRUE)

cat("<pre class='jamovitable'>")
print(jtable(unmasked_RTs_ttest_w$ttest))
cat("</pre>")

cat("<pre class='jamovitable'>")
print(jtable(unmasked_RTs_ttest_b$ttest))
cat("</pre>")

```



### Identification tasks

This section sought to show that participants could not recognise their own faces in the masked identification task. The measure used was $d'$ - the hits and false alarms are not given, so it isn't possible to reproduce the $d'$ calculations, but I assume they were correct. 

From the paper: 

>Participants performed at chance in identifying their own face in the masked identification task, $t(17) = 1.57, p = .135$, 95% CI for the mean difference
$= [−0.07, 0.5], BF = 0.68$ (null hypothesis 1.5 times more likely, anecdotal evidence). In contrast, $d'$ values were significantly different from 0 in the unmasked identification task, $t(17) = 3.85, p = .001$, 95% CI $= [0.73, 2.51], d = 0.91, BF = 23.98$ (alternative hypothesis 24 times more likely, strong evidence).

These are almost all replicated below, with the exeption of the BF of 23.98, which comes out at 29.98 in the analysis - I suspect this was a typo. 

```{r identification d`, masked trials, echo=FALSE, results = 'asis' }
identification_dPrime <- jmv::ttestOneS(
    data = mainData,
    vars = vars(Masked_D_prime, Umasked_D_prime),
    bf = FALSE,
    effectSize = TRUE,
    ci = TRUE)

identification_dPrime_bayes <- jmv::ttestOneS(
    data = mainData,
    vars = vars(Masked_D_prime, Umasked_D_prime),
    students = FALSE,
    bf = TRUE)

cat("<pre class='jamovitable'>")
print(jtable(identification_dPrime$ttest))
cat("</pre>")

cat("<pre class='jamovitable'>")
print(jtable(identification_dPrime_bayes$ttest))
cat("</pre>")

```

## ERP analyses

As I mentioned above, it isn't possible to replicate the actual ERPs, since EEG data and ERPs are not provided. However, the Excel file contains the extracted ERP values for each subject, so the statistical analyses can be reproduced. The authors looked at ipsilateral vs. contralateral N2pc values, for both the masked and unmasked dot-probe task conditions. For the unmasked task, they also looked at the late N2pc component. The analyses could all be replicated, but interestingly the Bayes factors reported are all for one-sided tests. 

### Masked dot-probe task

From the paper: 

>For the masked dot-probe task, a paired-samples t test (contralateral vs. ipsilateral) was performed to assess the presence of an early N2pc, $t(17) = −2.34, p = .031$, 95% CI for the mean difference between contralateral and ipsilateral amplitudes $= [−0.48, −0.03], d = −0.55, BF = 4.07$ (alternative hypothesis 4.1 times more likely, moderate evidence). It indicated that the overall mean amplitudes of the contralateral waveform were more negative ($M = −0.02$ $\mu V$) than the mean amplitudes of the ipsilateral waveform ($M = 0.23$ $\mu V$).

The analyses with two-sided Bayes tests are below, along with the t-tests:

```{r ERP analyses two-sided masked condition, echo = FALSE, results = 'asis'}

masked_ERP_ttest <- jmv::ttestPS(
    data = mainData,
    pairs = list(
        list(
            i1="Masked_contr_Early",
            i2="Masked_ipsi_Early")), 
    ci = TRUE, 
    desc = TRUE, 
    effectSize = TRUE)

masked_ERP_ttest_b <- jmv::ttestPS(
    data = mainData,
    pairs = list(
        list(
            i1="Masked_contr_Early",
            i2="Masked_ipsi_Early")),
    students = FALSE,
    bf = TRUE)

cat("<pre class='jamovitable'>")
print(jtable(masked_ERP_ttest$ttest))
cat("</pre>")

cat("<pre class='jamovitable'>")
print(jtable(masked_ERP_ttest_b$ttest))
cat("</pre>")

cat("<pre class='jamovitable'>")
print(jtable(masked_ERP_ttest$desc))
cat("</pre>")

```

The Bayes result can only be replicated with a one-sided test: 


```{r ERP analyses one-sided masked condition, echo = FALSE, results = 'asis'}


masked_ERP_ttest_b_one <- jmv::ttestPS(
    data = mainData,
    pairs = list(
        list(
            i1="Masked_contr_Early",
            i2="Masked_ipsi_Early")),
    students = FALSE,
    bf = TRUE, 
    hypothesis = "twoGreater" )


cat("<pre class='jamovitable'>")
print(jtable(masked_ERP_ttest_b_one$ttest))
cat("</pre>")
```

### Unmasked dot-probe task
Again, the analyses could be replicated, but only by running a one-sided Bayesian t-test. 

From the paper: 

> For the unmasked dot-probe task, a paired-samples t test (contralateral vs. ipsilateral) indicated a clear early N2pc component, as amplitudes of the contralateral waveforms were more negative ($M = 0.23$ $\mu V$) than the amplitudes of the ipsilateral waveforms ($M = 0.74$ $\mu V$), $t(17) = 2.91, p = .01$, 95% CI = $[−0.87, −0.14], d = −0.67, BF = 10.71$ (alternative hypothesis 10.7 times more likely, strong evidence)


```{r ERP analyses two-sided unmasked condition, echo = FALSE, results = 'asis'}

unmasked_ERP_ttest <- jmv::ttestPS(
    data = mainData,
    pairs = list(
        list(
            i1="Unmask_contr_Early",
            i2="Unmasked_Ipsi_Early")), 
    ci = TRUE, 
    desc = TRUE, 
    effectSize = TRUE)

unmasked_ERP_ttest_b <- jmv::ttestPS(
    data = mainData,
    pairs = list(
        list(
            i1="Unmask_contr_Early",
            i2="Unmasked_Ipsi_Early")),
    students = FALSE,
    bf = TRUE)

cat("<pre class='jamovitable'>")
print(jtable(unmasked_ERP_ttest$desc))
cat("</pre>")

cat("<pre class='jamovitable'>")
print(jtable(unmasked_ERP_ttest$ttest))
cat("</pre>")

cat("<pre class='jamovitable'>")
print(jtable(unmasked_ERP_ttest_b$ttest))
cat("</pre>")
```


Again, the Bayes result can only be replicated with a one-sided test: 

```{r ERP analyses one-sided unmasked condition, echo = FALSE, results = 'asis'}

unmasked_ERP_ttest_b_1 <- jmv::ttestPS(
    data = mainData,
    pairs = list(
        list(
            i1="Unmask_contr_Early",
            i2="Unmasked_Ipsi_Early")),
    students = FALSE,
    bf = TRUE, 
    hypothesis = "twoGreater" )


cat("<pre class='jamovitable'>")
print(jtable(unmasked_ERP_ttest_b_1$ttest))
cat("</pre>")
```

The authors then report the late N2pc component from the unmasked task (presumably this was not significant in the masked task as the data are not provided). 

From the paper: 

> A paired-samples t test was run (contralateral vs. ipsilateral) to test whether a late N2pc component was elicited. It showed that the amplitudes of the contralateral waveforms significantly differed (M = 3.24 μV) from the amplitudes of the ipsilateral waveforms ($M$ = 3.61 $\mu V$), $t(17) = 2.54, p = .021$, 95%
CI = $[−0.68, −0.06], d = −0.6, BF = 5.66$ (alternative hypothesis 5.7 times more likely, moderate evidence).



```{r ERP late analyses two-sided unmasked condition, echo = FALSE, results = 'asis'}

unmasked_ERP_ttest_late <- jmv::ttestPS(
    data = mainData,
    pairs = list(
        list(
            i1="Unmask_contr_Late",
            i2="Unmask_ipsi_Late")),
    ci = TRUE,
    desc = TRUE)

unmasked_ERP_ttest_late_b <- jmv::ttestPS(
    data = mainData,
    pairs = list(
        list(
            i1="Unmask_contr_Late",
            i2="Unmask_ipsi_Late")),
    students = FALSE,
    bf = TRUE)


cat("<pre class='jamovitable'>")
print(jtable(unmasked_ERP_ttest_late$desc))
cat("</pre>")

cat("<pre class='jamovitable'>")
print(jtable(unmasked_ERP_ttest_late$ttest))
cat("</pre>")

cat("<pre class='jamovitable'>")
print(jtable(unmasked_ERP_ttest_late_b$ttest))
cat("</pre>")
```


As above, the Bayes result could only be reproduced with a one-sided test. 


```{r ERP analyses one-sided unmasked late condition, echo = FALSE, results = 'asis'}

unmasked_ERP_ttest_late_b_1 <- jmv::ttestPS(
    data = mainData,
    pairs = list(
        list(
            i1="Unmask_contr_Late",
            i2="Unmask_ipsi_Late")),
    students = FALSE,
    bf = TRUE, 
    hypothesis = "twoGreater" )


cat("<pre class='jamovitable'>")
print(jtable(unmasked_ERP_ttest_late_b_1$ttest))
cat("</pre>")
```

The paper then reports a non-parametric cluster-level one-sample t-test analysis, but this is not possible to reproduce as the ERP data are not provided. 

## Validity of the masking procedure

The authors then report that they did a check on the validity of the masking procedure by comparing subjects who detected their own face above an (unstated) d' cutoff with those who did not, on their N2pc results. Leaving aside the fact that this was very underpowered (n=9 per group) and that a non-significant result does not indicate no difference, it was initially not possible to replicate these analyses because group assignment was not given. However, after some thought I realised I could use a median split on d' to reconstruct this analysis.

From the paper: 

> When we consider interindividual differences, it might be argued that some participants were conscious of the target presentation, and the early N2pc effect was influenced mainly by their data. There-fore, we divided the sample into two subgroups: One (n = 9) performed at chance level in the masked identification task (mean $d′$ = −0.24), and another (n = 9) per-formed above chance (mean $d′$ = 0.66). However, the group factor did not differentiate the N2pc amplitude, $t(16) = 0.58, p = .573, BF = 0.46$ (null hypothesis 2.2 times more likely, anecdotal evidence)"

```{r compare groups on N2pc, echo = FALSE, results = 'asis'}

# Compute Group assignment using median split

cutoff <- median(mainData$Masked_D_prime)
mainData$Group <- ifelse(mainData$Masked_D_prime >= cutoff, "Detected", "Not_Detected")

## t-test

N2pc_comparison_t <- jmv::ttestIS(
    formula = masked_N2pc_E ~ Group,
    data = mainData,
    vars = vars(masked_N2pc_E),
    students = TRUE)

# Bayesian t-test 
N2pc_comparison_b <- jmv::ttestIS(
    formula = masked_N2pc_E ~ Group,
    data = mainData,
    vars = vars(masked_N2pc_E),
    students = FALSE,
    bf = TRUE)

# Descriptives 
DPrime_comparison <- jmv::ttestIS(
    formula = Masked_D_prime ~ Group,
    data = mainData,
    vars = vars(Masked_D_prime),
    bf = FALSE,
    desc = TRUE)

# print tables 
cat("<pre class='jamovitable'>")
print(jtable(DPrime_comparison$desc))
cat("</pre>")

cat("<pre class='jamovitable'>")
print(jtable(N2pc_comparison_t$ttest))
cat("</pre>")

cat("<pre class='jamovitable'>")
print(jtable(N2pc_comparison_b$ttest))
cat("</pre>")

```

## N2pc and d' correlation

The authors also looked at the correlations between d-prime and the N2pc component, and although they again make the error that a non-significant results indicates no relationship, I was able to replicate these correlations. 

From the paper: 

> Further, the amplitude of the early N2pc component observed in the masked dot-probe task did not correlate with the $d′$ obtained in the masked identification task, $r = −.2, p = .424, BF = 0.39$ (null hypothesis 2.6 times more likely, anecdotal evidence), indicating no relation between visibility and attention shifts. In contrast, the amplitude of the early N2pc component elicited in the unmasked dot-probe task correlated negatively with the $d′$ measured in the unmasked identification task, $r = −.58, p = .011, BF = 5.87$ (alternative hypothesis 5.9 times more likely, moderate evidence)

All of these can be seen in the tables below. 

```{r correlations, echo=FALSE}
jmv::corrMatrix(
    data = mainData,
    vars = vars(masked_N2pc_E, Masked_D_prime))

```

```{r Bayesian correlation matrix, echo = FALSE}

# NOTE: For this analysis, it is necessary to install jsq which is not yet on CRAN: remotes::install_github('jonathon-love/jsq')
# might also be necessary to install jmvcore and reboot R; remotes::install_github('jamovi/jmvcore')

jsq::bcorrMatrix(
    data = mainData,
    vars = vars(masked_N2pc_E, Masked_D_prime))

```

```{r correlations unmasked, echo=FALSE}
jmv::corrMatrix(
    data = mainData,
    vars = vars(unmasked_N2pc_E, Umasked_D_prime))


```


```{r Bayesian correlation matrix unmasked, echo = FALSE}
# Necessary to install jsq which is not yet on CRAN: remotes::install_github('jonathon-love/jsq')
# might also be necessary to install jmvcore and reboot R; remotes::install_github('jamovi/jmvcore')

jsq::bcorrMatrix(
    data = mainData,
    vars = vars(unmasked_N2pc_E, Umasked_D_prime),
    plotDens = TRUE,
    plotPost = TRUE)

```


## Behavioural control experiment

The authors also report a behavioural control experiment with the tasks in reverse order (n = 17), but they do not provide the data for this, so it is not possible to replicate the analyses. 


## Overall summary

It is possible to replicate most of the statistical analyses in the paper, although there appears to have been a bit of "B-hacking" with regard to the Bayesian analyses. The ERP results cannot be reproduced as the EEG data are not provided; nor are the data for the behavioural control experiment.
